74-019.r: Major coal reserves (1 April 2023): Odisha 100.99 billion t, Jharkhand 93.25, Chhattisgarh 85.26 → all the above.

74-021.r: Coal reserves when asked: Jharkhand > Odisha > Chhattisgarh > Madhya Pradesh (a). 1 April 2023: Odisha > Jharkhand > Chhattisgarh > West Bengal > Madhya Pradesh.

74-022.r: Proved coal reserves (1-4-2014): Jharkhand > Odisha > Chhattisgarh > Madhya Pradesh. Resources 1 April 2023 (billion t): Odisha 100.99, Jharkhand 93.25, Chhattisgarh 85.26, West Bengal 34.39, MP 33.56.

74-023.r: Coal output 2014-15: Chhattisgarh 22.5% > Jharkhand 20.0% > Odisha 19.9% (> Maharashtra). 2024-25: Odisha > Jharkhand > Chhattisgarh > Madhya Pradesh > Telangana.

74-024.r: Chota Nagpur industrial region (Jharkhand, north Odisha, West Bengal; heavy metallurgy) → grew from the discovery of coal in the Damodar Valley.

74-025.r: Jharkhand's share of India's coal output (2024-25): 19.68% → none of the options (40–49%) fits; the book gives no single answer (*).

74-026.r: Coal output 2008-09: Chhattisgarh 20.7% > Odisha 20.0% > Jharkhand 19.5%. 2024-25: Odisha 25.71%, Jharkhand 19.68%, Chhattisgarh 19.56%, Madhya Pradesh 15.99%.

74-028.r: Korba coalfield → Korba district, Chhattisgarh, in the Hasdeo river basin.

74-029.r: Coal valleys: Damodar → Barakar; Son → Umaria; Godavari → Singareni; Mahanadi → Talcher.

74-030.r: Talcher → Mahanadi valley; Karanpura → Damodar valley; Singrauli → Son valley; Singareni → Godavari valley.
74-030.t: Don't confuse Singrauli (Son valley) with Singareni (Godavari valley).

74-031.r: Wrong pair: Madhya Pradesh–Singareni; Singareni is in Telangana. Correct: Odisha–Talcher, Chhattisgarh–Korba, Maharashtra–Wardha Valley.

74-032.r: Talcher coalfield → Angul district, Odisha; managed by Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd., a Coal India subsidiary.

74-034.r: Chota Nagpur's share in coal output: about 80% when asked; 68.39% now (2024-25). Spread over Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, West Bengal.

74-035.r: Jharia (Dhanbad, Jharkhand) → coal mines, most coking coal reserves. Jamshedpur → iron and steel; Lohardaga → bauxite; Ranchi → heavy machines.

74-036.r: Coal reserves (IMYB 2015, million t): Raniganj 24632.83 (WB) + 2036.30 (Jharkhand) > Jharia 19430.06 > Singrauli 14803.52 > Korba 11755.66. Jharia (Jharkhand) → coal.

74-039.r: Lignite → inferior coal (book: 40–55% carbon); mainly produced in Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Rajasthan (Neyveli in TN), not Jharkhand → R false.
74-039.c: Sources give lignite's carbon content differently (the book itself says 40–55%), so A is accepted as broadly true; the decisive point is R: Tamil Nadu (Neyveli), not Jharkhand, leads lignite output.

74-040.r: Lignite → Tamil Nadu leads; production 2024-25: Tamil Nadu 48.65%, Gujarat 29.46%, Rajasthan 21.88%.

74-041.r: Neyveli (Tamil Nadu) → India's largest lignite field; Tamil Nadu tops lignite reserves and production.

74-042.r: Largest lignite reserves → Tamil Nadu; India's lignite reserves/resources: 47.36 billion tonnes (1 April 2023).

74-043.r: Bengal-Jharkhand coalfields supply the north-western states by rail, so coal is a major part of inter-state rail traffic → A and R true, R explains A.

74-045.r: Karanpura → Jharkhand; Singareni → Andhra Pradesh (now Telangana); Neyveli → Tamil Nadu; Korba → Chhattisgarh.

74-046.r: India imports coal because coal-based power plants lack enough domestic supply and steel makers need good coking coal → 2 and 3; there is no policy of saving reserves.

74-047.r: Neither: coalbed methane → ~90% pure methane from coal seams; shale gas → over 86% methane, not just propane-butane; India has shale gas (Indo-Gangetic plain, Assam, Gujarat, Rajasthan).

74-048.r: Indian coal industry problems: poor-quality coal, movement bottlenecks, low washery use, rising coking-coal imports, administered prices → all four.

74-049.r: Most coal in India is used for energy (power) production.

74-050.r: Jharkhand lacks major lignite reserves. Lignite (brown coal): high moisture, low ash, low heating value; reserves mainly Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan, Gujarat (1 April 2023).

74-051.r: Damodar valley → largest Gondwana coal reserves: Jharia, Dhanbad, Bokaro (Jharkhand) and Raniganj (West Bengal, extending into Jharkhand).

74-052.r: Rajmahal → Jharkhand (and Bihar); Sohagpur → Madhya Pradesh (and Chhattisgarh); Bisrampur → Chhattisgarh; Raniganj → West Bengal (and Jharkhand).

74-053.r: Wrong: Mawlong is in Meghalaya (East Khasi Hills), not Arunachal. Correct: Raniganj–West Bengal, Ramgarh–Jharkhand, Talcher–Odisha (Angul) → 2, 3 and 4.

74-054.r: Makum → Assam; Namchik(-Namphuk) → Arunachal Pradesh (Changlang); Giridih → Jharkhand (best-quality coal); Sohagpur → Madhya Pradesh.

74-055.r: Namchik-Namphuk coalfields → Changlang district, Arunachal Pradesh.

74-056.r: Jhilmili → Chhattisgarh; Karanpura → Jharkhand; Rampur Himgir → Odisha; Sohagpur → Madhya Pradesh (and Chhattisgarh).

74-057.r: Ranjit Valley → Sikkim; Tandur → Telangana; Warora → Maharashtra; Lalmatia → Jharkhand.

74-058.r: Coal resources (1-4-2023, million t): Hutar → Jharkhand (249.82); Ib River → Odisha (39830.07); Tatapani-Ramkola → Chhattisgarh (80773.87); Umaria → Madhya Pradesh (181.29).

74-059.r: Underground coal burning (coal fire) → Jharia coalfield, Jharkhand.

74-060.r: Coal Controller's Organisation (1916): main coal statistics source (Statistics Act 2008), monitors captive coal/lignite blocks, hears objections on coal-land acquisition (1957 Act) → 1, 2, 3; not coal-delivery timelines.

75-001.r: Digboi (Assam) → India's oldest oil field; the Brahmaputra valley is the oldest oil basin.

75-002.r: Crude oil 2024-25 (P, thousand tonnes): Gujarat 5135 > Assam 4452 > Rajasthan 3429; Gujarat was also the leader when asked.

75-003.r: Largest crude oil producer → Gujarat (in 2013-14, as asked, and again in 2024-25).

75-004.r: Ankleshwar (Bharuch district, Gujarat) → petroleum reserves; area about 38.98 km².

75-005.r: Lunej (Cambay basin) → oil-producing area in Gujarat; oil occurs in Tertiary sedimentary rocks.

75-006.r: Navgam oil field → Gujarat; other Gujarat oil fields: Ankleshwar, Kalol, Bakrol, Mehsana.

75-007.r: First oil well in India → Makum, upper Assam, 26 March 1867 (118 feet, 35.9 m). The book calls the Commission's revised key (Digboi) wrong.

75-008.r: Oldest refinery → Digboi (1901). Then Koyali, Gujarat (1965); Haldia, West Bengal (1975); Mathura, Uttar Pradesh (1982).

75-009.r: Correct pair: Visakhapatnam refinery (HPCL) → Andhra Pradesh. Barauni is in Bihar, Mathura in Uttar Pradesh; Koyna has no refinery.

75-010.r: Correct pair: Panagudi → Tamil Nadu. Haldia → West Bengal; Jamnagar → Gujarat (Reliance, world's largest refinery); Numaligarh → Golaghat, Assam.

75-012.r: Hatia (Jharkhand) has no oil refinery; Koyali, Noonmati and Barauni do.

75-013.r: First oil/energy crisis → 1973, when OPEC suddenly raised oil prices four times → during the 1970s and 1980s.

75-015.r: Refineries: Haldia → West Bengal; Jamnagar → Gujarat; Kochi → Kerala; Numaligarh → Assam.

75-016.r: Numaligarh → Assam; Tatipaka → Andhra Pradesh; Koyali → Gujarat; Barauni → Bihar.

75-017.r: Tatipaka refinery → Tatipaka village, Konaseema region, Andhra Pradesh; set up by ONGC.

75-018.r: Nayara (Vadinar) → Gujarat; Manali (CPCL, Chennai) → Tamil Nadu; Numaligarh (Golaghat) → Assam; Tatipaka (ONGC, Konaseema) → Andhra Pradesh.

75-020.r: Noonmati → Assam; Koyali → Gujarat; Mangalore → Karnataka; Panipat → Haryana.

75-021.r: Tatipaka → Andhra Pradesh; Koyali → Gujarat; Nagapattinam → Tamil Nadu; Numaligarh → Assam.

75-022.r: Wrong pair: Koyali (Gujarat)–HPCL; Koyali is an IOCL refinery. Correct: Bina–BPCL (& OOCL), Tatipaka–ONGC, Digboi–IOCL.
